# sloop

> sloop is a command-line tool that registers your PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB databases once, then backs them up, restores them, mirrors them, syncs them and keeps all of it on a schedule — on Windows, Linux and macOS, without your credentials ever leaving the machine.

## What people get wrong first

### The guarantee is structural, not a policy

sloop cannot send your credentials anywhere, because it cannot send anything anywhere.
There is no HTTP client in its dependency graph, and no SSH client either. CI fails the
build on the day one appears. Anyone can check it:

    cargo tree --manifest-path cli/Cargo.toml | grep -Ei 'reqwest|hyper|ureq|curl'

The two jobs that need a network run programs the machine already has — the system
curl to fetch client tools, and the system ssh to reach a firewalled database — and
only after the user agrees. There is no telemetry, no analytics and no update check.

### mirror and sync are different commands

mirror makes the destination identical to the source. Anything that existed only in
the destination is gone. sync merges: rows are added, rows already there are replaced,
and rows that exist only in the destination are kept. Picking the wrong one is the
mistake the documentation is arranged to prevent.

Both are same-engine. Copying between engines is refused, deliberately and with a
reason, and it is not on the roadmap.

## What it is

One binary. No agent to deploy, no server to run, no account to make.

Engines      PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB
Platforms    Windows, Linux, macOS — x86_64 and aarch64
Crate        dbsloop        Binary   sloop        Licence   MIT OR Apache-2.0

Run `sloop` with no arguments for an interactive menu covering every command; run it
with flags for the same thing from a scheduler. The menu does not reimplement anything —
each screen collects what a flag carries and calls the same function — and every
interactive run ends by printing the flag form of what it just did, so a session becomes
a line you can schedule.

Passwords are never stored in plaintext and never appear in argv, so never in `ps`. A
registry holds a route — OS keyring, an Argon2id-encrypted file, an environment variable,
or a command to run — and never a value.

## Pages

- [sloop](https://dbsloop.github.io/): A database operations CLI for PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. Register a database once, then back it up, restore it, mirror it or sync it — from a menu or from a flag, with no HTTP client anywhere in the binary.
- [Documentation](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/): Every page of the sloop documentation, by section: installing it, registering databases, backups and restores, copying, the background service, and the reference.

### Start here

Get sloop onto the machine, and a verified backup out of it.

- [Installation](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/install/): The one-liner for your platform, what it does to PATH, and both ways to take sloop off again.
- [Getting started](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/getting-started/): From an empty machine to a verified backup you can restore, in six commands.

### Databases

Registering them, and knowing which registry a bare name resolves to.

- [Databases, registries and projects](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/databases/): Register a database once, then name it. Where that name is looked up, and what happens when two registries both hold it.
- [Reaching a database over SSH](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/ssh/): A database whose port is closed, reached by running the machine’s own ssh — never a client built into the binary.

### Backups

Taking them, proving them, keeping them, and putting one back.

- [Backups, retention and restoring](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/backups/): Take one, prove every row arrived, delete what is past its retention, and put it back when you need it.
- [The backup key](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/backup-key/): An age keypair, and the asymmetry is the point: a scheduled backup needs no secret, and only a restore does.

### Copying

Two commands that are not the same command.

- [Mirror and sync](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/mirror-and-sync/): One makes the destination identical to the source. The other merges into what is already there. Picking the wrong one is the mistake this page exists to stop.

### Reading

Looking inside a database without writing any SQL.

- [Reading a database](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/query/): Pick a table, tick the columns, choose the test. Nothing it runs can write, and the server is what guarantees that.

### The background service

The feature that replaces cron, on all three platforms.

- [The background service](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/service/): sloop registers itself with your machine and backs your databases up on a schedule, with nobody logged in.
- [Activity and monitoring](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/activity/): Rows in, rows out and size, per database per day — and the one number no engine will give you.

### This machine

What sloop puts on it, and how to take all of it off.

- [sloop’s own PostgreSQL](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/postgres/): The registry, the schedules and the service’s readings live in a PostgreSQL 18 of sloop’s own. Here is how to open it yourself.
- [Reset and uninstall](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/reset/): Put the machine back to the moment sloop was installed — and the one thing that can still be lost.

### Reference

Every flag, every exit code, and how to check the claim yourself.

- [Command reference](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/commands/): Every command and every flag, checked against --help rather than remembered.
- [Security](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/security/): The guarantee, expanded — and how to check it yourself in thirty seconds.
- [The privileges a backup role needs](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/privileges/): What a role has to be able to do per engine, what breaks silently without it, and the GRANT that fixes it.
- [Automation](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/automation/): Running sloop from something that is not a person: exit codes, non-interactive flags, and output a script can read.
- [Roadmap](https://dbsloop.github.io/docs/roadmap/): What is planned. No dates, and nothing that reads as a promise.

## Questions

### Does sloop upload my databases or credentials anywhere?

No, and it could not. There is no HTTP client in the binary. Backups are written to
disk on the machine that took them.

### Do I need cron, systemd timers or Task Scheduler?

No. `sloop service install` registers sloop with the machine’s own service manager —
a systemd unit, a launchd daemon, or a real Windows service — and it takes the backups
itself with nobody logged in. Nothing is written to crontab or Task Scheduler. If you
would rather drive it from a scheduler you already have, sloop is an ordinary command
and the automation page has a recipe for each.

### How do I know a backup is good?

Every row is counted on both sides, per table, with one statement, and a table that did
not arrive is a failure. Planner estimates are available as SLOOP_VERIFY=fast, are
always labelled an estimate, and are never presented as proof. Exit 6 means the run
finished and then the counts disagreed — neither success nor a crash, which is why it
has a number of its own.

### Can it copy a PostgreSQL database into MySQL?

No. mirror, sync and restore all refuse across engines, and each says why rather than
pointing at a ticket: the type systems do not map cleanly, and a copy that quietly
rounds or truncates is worse than one that refuses.

### What happens to a scheduled run that needs an answer?

It never asks. When standard input is not a terminal, a command that needs an answer
exits 2 and names the exact flag that would have given it. -y answers a question,
--force overrides a refusal, and --confirm <name> is the only way to destroy something
named — and none of the three stands in for another.

### Does uninstalling it delete my backups?

No. Not `sloop reset`, not `sloop uninstall`, not ever. They are the one thing on a
machine that cannot be regenerated. What can still be lost is the ability to read an
encrypted one: export the backup key before you reset.

### Does it need administrator rights?

Only to register or start the background service, and it asks before it does anything
rather than failing halfway. Everything sloop installs goes under ~/.sloop; nothing is
put in Program Files or /usr/local.
